proposedTopics.title: Maximal Extractable Value (MEV)
proposedTopics.description: MEV is value extracted from block production beyond standard block rewards and gas fees by including, excluding, or changing transaction order: PBS, the searcher→builder→proposer supply chain, and arbitrage, liquidation, and sandwich strategies.

proposedTopics.title: Intents & ERC-7683
proposedTopics.description: Intents shift the model from signing prescribed calls toward authorizing constraints or desired outcomes that solvers compete to fulfill: generalized smart-account intents, ERC-7683's solver-facing order representation, and UniswapX/CoW/Across solver markets.

proposedTopics.title: Uniswap V4 Hooks (Deep)
proposedTopics.description: V4 hooks are pool-specific extension contracts: before/after lifecycle callbacks, dynamic LP fees, permission bits encoded in the hook address, return deltas, and production hook design patterns.

proposedTopics.title: Proposer-builder separation (PBS)
proposedTopics.description: PBS splits block building from block proposing: builders assemble execution payloads and bid, while the selected validator chooses a blinded payload header before the body is revealed. MEV-Boost implements out-of-protocol PBS through trusted relays; EIP-7732 is a draft proposal for enshrined PBS. Outsourcing specialized building lets solo validators compete for builder revenue without running the same MEV infrastructure.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/pbs.md diagram the proposer↔relay↔builder flow and explain what the proposer commits to (a header) before it sees the body. Done when: you can state why PBS uses a commit-reveal via a trusted relay and what a proposer could steal without one (unbundling/frontrunning the builder's MEV).

proposedTopics.title: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers
proposedTopics.description: MEV flows through specialized actors: searchers identify opportunities and submit ordered bundles or private transactions, builders combine private order flow with public transactions into valuable blocks, relays validate and escrow builder payloads, and proposers choose among header bids. Competition can bid much of an opportunity's value toward the proposer, but the exact split is market-dependent.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/mev-supply-chain.md trace one sandwich opportunity from a searcher's bundle through a builder and relay to a proposer, labelling data visibility, bids, and possible revenue at each step. Done when: you can explain why competition can bid most of a highly contested opportunity toward the proposer without assuming that split for every opportunity.

proposedTopics.title: Flashbots & MEV-Boost
proposedTopics.description: Flashbots Auction provides private submission of ordered transaction bundles to builders, while MEV-Boost lets validators query relays for competing builder headers. A bundle targets a block and executes in order; transactions revert the bundle unless explicitly allowed to revert, but inclusion is never guaranteed. Private sealed bidding avoids public-mempool priority-gas auctions and losing bids staying onchain, while builders and relays still see order flow and can censor it.

proposedTopics.title: Arbitrage & sandwich MEV
proposedTopics.description: DEX arbitrage buys on the lower-priced venue and sells on the higher-priced venue in one atomic transaction, subject to fees, gas, competition, and execution. A sandwich places one trade before a visible victim swap to worsen its execution and another after it to unwind; the victim's size and permitted price movement bound the opportunity.

proposedTopics.title: Liquidation MEV
proposedTopics.description: In Aave V3, a position becomes liquidatable when its health factor falls below 1. A liquidator repays eligible debt and receives corresponding collateral plus the configured liquidation bonus; bots compete on monitoring, oracle updates, execution cost, and inclusion. A flash loan can supply temporary debt capital, but its premium, swaps, gas, and slippage still determine profitability.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/Liquidator.sol implement a flashLoanSimple receiver that calls liquidationCall against a pinned local Aave V3 fixture, then swaps enough seized collateral to repay principal plus premium. Done when: forge test moves the fixture's oracle price below health factor 1 and proves the debt reduction, collateral seizure, flash-loan repayment, and positive net balance atomically. Preserved substantial practice (180 minutes, split across sessions): Practice building a flash-loan-funded liquidation bot (Damn Vulnerable DeFi puppet-style / real Aave). Flash-borrow the debt asset, call liquidationCall, seize collateral, swap enough to repay principal plus premium, and keep only the net remainder — all atomically in a pinned local fixture. Reference: https://github.com/aave-dao/aave-v3-origin/blob/main/src/contracts/interfaces/IPool.sol. Save executable evidence and a next step; schedule a later changed-case independent check. The short recall card does not mark this build complete.

proposedTopics.title: Intents & solvers
proposedTopics.description: An intent authorizes constraints or outcomes rather than necessarily prescribing one calldata path. Solvers search for valid executions and submit solution transactions, but there is no single universal intent format: authorization, nonce/replay rules, settlement, and solver payment belong to the chosen standard and protocol. Smart-account intent proposals such as ERC-7521 separate wallet signature validation from intent-standard execution.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/intents.md contrast an imperative transaction with an ERC-7521 UserIntent and IntentSolution, including wallet validation, segments, solver simulation, nonce/replay policy, deadline, chain, assets, and minimum outcome. Done when: you can identify which constraints are signature-bound and which trust assumptions come from the selected intent standard and settlement protocol.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-7683 cross-chain intents
proposedTopics.description: The current ERC-7683 draft standardizes a solver-facing representation, not a universal open/fill settlement interface. A protocol exposes an opaque payload and an onchain resolver that solvers call offchain to obtain ordered steps, variables, payments, and named assumptions. The protocol still chooses authorization, order dissemination, pricing, execution ordering, settlement verification, and payment security.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/erc7683.md map protocol payload → vetted resolver eth_call → ResolvedOrder steps/variables/payments/assumptions → solver execution, and contrast it with the superseded open/fill draft. Done when: you can explain what ERC-7683 guarantees, what a resolver must surface, and why settlement safety remains protocol-specific.

proposedTopics.title: V4 beforeSwap & afterSwap callbacks
proposedTopics.description: A V4 hook is an external contract attached to a pool and called by PoolManager at address-permissioned lifecycle points. beforeSwap can alter the specified/unspecified deltas only when the corresponding return-delta flag is set and may return a per-swap LP-fee override for dynamic-fee pools; afterSwap can return an unspecified-currency delta when permissioned. Every callback must return its selector, and resulting deltas participate in PoolManager accounting.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/LogHook.sol implement a hook overriding beforeSwap and afterSwap that records swap counts, and test it against a v4 PoolManager in test/phase09/LogHook.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves both callbacks fire on a swap and the hook returns the correct selector (returning the wrong selector must revert the pool call).

proposedTopics.title: V4 dynamic fees via hooks
proposedTopics.description: A V4 pool's dynamic-fee capability is immutable at initialization and encoded by LPFeeLibrary.DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG (0x800000). Its hook can update the stored LP fee through PoolManager.updateDynamicLPFee or return a valid per-swap override from beforeSwap with OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG. These are LP fees, distinct from protocol fees and custom hook fees.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/DynamicFeeHook.sol set a higher fee when a swap pushes price in one direction and a lower fee otherwise, tested in test/phase09/DynamicFeeHook.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves two identical-size swaps in opposite directions are charged different fees, and the pool was created with the dynamic-fee sentinel.

proposedTopics.title: V4 hook permission flags & address mining
proposedTopics.description: The 14 least-significant bits of a V4 hook address encode callback and return-delta permissions. PoolManager checks these bits to decide which callbacks to invoke; BaseHook's constructor validates that the deployed address matches getHookPermissions. CREATE2 salt mining is therefore used to deploy at an address with the intended bitmap.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/HookMiner.t.sol use HookMiner to find a CREATE2 salt for BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG | AFTER_SWAP_FLAG, deploy the hook, and initialize a pool with it. Done when: forge test proves the deployed address bitmap and callback execution, while deploying BaseHook bytecode at an address inconsistent with getHookPermissions reverts during construction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does PBS separate, and what does the proposer actually commit to?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Builders assemble execution payloads and bid; the proposer chooses a blinded header before body reveal. Today MEV-Boost implements this out of protocol through trusted relays, while EIP-7732 is only a draft for enshrined PBS. The commitment prevents same-slot unbundling of a revealed builder payload.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers
proposedPrompts.promptText: Trace MEV through its actors and say where most of the value ends up.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Searchers submit bundles/private transactions → builders combine them with public flow → relays validate and escrow candidate payloads → proposers choose header bids. Competition can move much of an opportunity's value to the proposer, but the realized split varies by opportunity and market structure.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does sending a bundle through Flashbots (vs the public mempool) give you, and what's the systemic cost?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: eth_sendBundle privately sends an ordered bundle for a target block; transactions revert the bundle unless listed in revertingTxHashes, and inclusion is not guaranteed. Losing sealed bids need not land onchain, but builders and relays can see or censor the order flow. MEV-Boost lets proposers choose competing builder headers through relays.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a sandwich attack profit, and what defeats it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Frontrun the victim's swap to push price against them, let them execute at the worse price, then backrun to unwind. The victim's size and permitted price movement bound the opportunity; fees, gas, competition, and execution determine realized profit. A tight minAmountOut can make the controlled example revert or unprofitable, while loose slippage creates more room for extraction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why do searchers race to liquidate, and how can a flash loan fund the transaction?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: On Aave V3, health factor below 1 permits liquidationCall: repay eligible debt and receive corresponding collateral plus the configured bonus. A flash loan can front the debt asset, but principal, premium, swap slippage, gas, and inclusion competition all must fit inside the realized bonus.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In 10 minutes, trace a flash-funded liquidation balance sheet. What must be true for the transaction to repay and leave a profit, and which change makes it revert?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Track debt repaid, collateral seized, executable sale proceeds, premium and gas separately. Repayment needs available debt tokens; slippage, close-factor bounds or a recovered health factor can invalidate the operation.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an order-flow auction return MEV to users?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: MEV-Share's mev_sendBundle can disclose selected privacy.hints so searchers compose backruns, then validity.refund and refundConfig allocate percentages after inclusion. More hints improve searchability but leak more; selected builders still receive the full submitted bundle.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an intent differ from a transaction, and what must the signature bound?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A transaction prescribes execution, while an intent authorizes constraints/outcomes that a solver may satisfy with a chosen path. The signed domain must bind the account, chain(s), assets, limits, deadline, and replay policy. Authorization and settlement security depend on the chosen intent standard; there is no universal intent envelope.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does the current ERC-7683 draft standardize, and what does it leave protocol-specific?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The current ERC-7683 draft standardizes opaque payload resolution into steps, variables, payments, and named assumptions through a vetted resolver called offchain with eth_call. It does not require a common open/fill interface or secure settlement; those remain protocol-specific.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Contrast UniswapX, CoW, and Across on price discovery and risk.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: UniswapX uses chain-specific competitive auctions, including Dutch output decay; CoW uses fair combinatorial batch auctions with coincidence-of-wants matching; Across relayers front destination capital and are repaid through bonded optimistic bundle settlement. Compare who sets price, fronts capital, and bears settlement/finality risk.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do V4's swap hooks fire, and what must a hook return?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: beforeSwap and afterSwap run around PoolManager.swap only when their address bits are set. Return-delta permissions are separate bits; beforeSwap may also return a per-swap LP-fee override for a dynamic-fee pool. Every callback returns its exact selector, and wrong selectors or malformed return data revert.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a V4 pool get a dynamic fee?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Initialize with LPFeeLibrary.DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG (0x800000); the hook may update the stored LP fee with updateDynamicLPFee or return a valid beforeSwap override carrying OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG. Dynamic capability is immutable, and LP fees are distinct from protocol and hook fees.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: V4 hook permission flags & address mining
proposedPrompts.promptText: How does the PoolManager know which hooks to call, and why must you mine the hook address?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Fourteen low address bits encode callback and return-delta permissions, so CREATE2 salt mining finds an address with the intended mask. BaseHook validates getHookPermissions against that address during construction; PoolManager later uses the bits to decide which callbacks to invoke.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What must a production V4 hook get right, and why is gas-leanness non-negotiable?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Extend BaseHook, make getHookPermissions match the mined address, restrict privileged entry points, and prove every returned delta settles under PoolManager accounting. Review callback inputs, nested actions/reentrancy, price manipulation, gas/DoS, and upgrade/admin risk; custom hook safety is not guaranteed by v4 core.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In 10 minutes, explain how a V4 hook address, permission flags and callback implementation agree. Name one test that catches a mismatch without rebuilding the full hook.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Map required callbacks to address flags and returned permissions; run one swap through the pinned PoolManager fixture, check callback execution, and test wrong permissions or unexpected sender.
